summary: Solid-carbon thermal batteries for round-the-clock industrial heat and power.
editor_note: Industrial storage gets more interesting when the battery is a hot block, not a scarce-mineral chemistry. Antora resistively heats solid carbon to 2,400°C, stores energy for multiple days, and began delivering energy from a 5 GWh POET project in under 12 months. Unlike lithium-ion systems optimized for shorter electrical cycles, this bet targets continuous factory heat and firm power with factory-built modules. The risk is whether those project economics repeat beyond the flagship site.

product_evidence.claim: Antora says its thermal battery resistively heats solid carbon to as high as 2,400°C, stores that energy for multiple days, and can return it as industrial heat or electricity through a steam turbine.
The official technology surface says factory-built modules scale from megawatts to gigawatts and use domestic, earth-abundant solid carbon rather than supply-constrained critical minerals.

Project Big Stone is a 5 GWh, 50 MW thermal-battery project with more than 200 modules under a POET energy offtake agreement; Antora says it advanced from an empty lot to first energy delivery in under 12 months.

market_context.primary_user: Industrial operators, data-center developers, utilities, and energy project teams that need firm heat or power at large scale.
market_context.differentiation: Antora stores electricity in abundant solid carbon and ships modular systems that can deliver both process heat and power, instead of relying on lithium electrochemistry for every load.
market_context.why_now: Industrial electrification and data-center growth are increasing demand for firm energy that can be deployed faster than new generation and transmission infrastructure.

risks.claim: The falsifiable risk is whether Antora can repeat Project Big Stone's sub-12-month delivery pace and economics across different industrial sites and duty cycles.
risks.basis: VentureDex editorial assessment based on the official technology, project, and Series C surfaces.
